questions.q: Distinguish between concave and convex mirrors and give their uses.
answer: Spherical mirrors are of two kinds, concave and convex, which behave very differently.

answer.text: A concave mirror has its reflecting surface curved inwards and is a converging mirror, because it brings parallel rays of light to a focus. Depending on where the object is placed, it can form a real and inverted image or a magnified virtual image. It is used in torches, vehicle headlights and searchlights to produce parallel beams, in shaving mirrors, by dentists, and in solar furnaces.

A convex mirror has its reflecting surface curved outwards and is a diverging mirror. It always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image, and gives a wide field of view. For this reason it is used as a rear-view mirror in vehicles, allowing the driver to see a large area behind.

answer: Thus their opposite curvatures give them opposite behaviours and uses.

questions.q: What is refraction of light, and why does it occur? Give everyday examples.

answer.text: Refraction is the bending of a ray of light when it passes from one transparent medium into another, for instance from air into water or glass.

Refraction occurs because light travels at different speeds in different media. When light enters a denser medium such as water, it slows down and bends towards the normal, and when it enters a rarer medium it speeds up and bends away from the normal. The extent of bending depends on the refractive index of the media.

A pencil placed in a glass of water appears bent at the surface, a swimming pool looks shallower than it really is, and letters under a glass slab seem raised. The twinkling of stars is also caused by refraction of light in the atmosphere.

answer: Refraction thus explains many common optical effects.

questions.q: How does a convex lens form images, and how do these change with the position of the object?

answer.text: is a converging lens, and the image it forms depends on how far the object is placed from it.

list: When the object is very far, a small, real, inverted image forms at the focus
As the object moves closer, the real image grows larger and moves farther from the lens
When the object is at twice the focal length, the image is real, inverted and of the same size
When the object is between the lens and its focus, the image is virtual, erect and enlarged — as in a magnifying glass

questions.q: State the laws of refraction and explain the role of the refractive index.

answer.text: is the bending of light as it passes from one transparent medium into another, and it follows definite laws.

list: The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane
The ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is constant for a given pair of media (Snell's law)

answer.text: measures how much a medium bends light.

list: It compares the speed of light in a vacuum with its speed in the medium
A higher refractive index, as in glass or diamond, means the medium bends and slows light more
